problem: The back-bearing formula is garbled and its second case is missing entirely: the text reads 'BB = FB + 180° if FB  180°'. A student cannot tell what happens when FB is larger than 180°, which is exactly the case tested in worked example 1 and quiz Q4.
fix: BB = FB + 180° if FB < 180°; BB = FB − 180° if FB ≥ 180°. (Equivalently, add or subtract 180° so the result stays between 0° and 360°.)

problem: The model answer repeats the same broken formula, 'BB = FB + 180° if FB  180°', so an examiner marking by this key would accept an incomplete relation and a student revising from it learns only half the rule.
fix: The two differ by 180°: BB = FB + 180° when FB < 180°, and BB = FB − 180° when FB ≥ 180°.

problem: 'An azimuth is the same angle measured clockwise from a north reference' is loose: a bearing may be a reduced bearing measured from the nearer end of the meridian, which is not the same angle as a clockwise azimuth from north.
fix: A bearing is the angle between a survey line and a stated meridian, and may be written whole circle or reduced. An azimuth is always measured clockwise from a north reference, usually true north, so it is the same as the whole circle bearing from that north.

problem: The declination rule is given only as an arithmetic sign. A student can apply it but cannot check it, because the chapter never says that for east declination the magnetic bearing is smaller than the true bearing, so the true meridian lies to the west of magnetic north.
fix: Add: with 5°30′ east declination, magnetic north lies 5°30′ east of true north, so every magnetic bearing reads smaller than the true bearing by that amount; the magnetic needle points to the right of true north.
